title: Jumble Puzzle Bins
story: You set the weekly word jumble for a local paper. The best puzzles are sets of words built from exactly the same letters, like least, slate and stale: readers get the scrambled letters and must find every word.
Readers mail in word suggestions, and you have a long list of them. You want to sort them into bins, one bin per set of letters, so you can see at a glance which bins are big enough for a puzzle.
task: Write groupJumbles(words). Put two words in the same bin exactly when one is a rearrangement of the other: the same letters, each used the same number of times. Return the list of bins.

Order matters, so the answer is unique. Bins appear in the order their first word appears in words. Inside a bin, words keep their order from words. If a word is suggested twice, both copies go in its bin. An empty list gives [].
constraints: Words contain only lowercase letters a to z.

examples.explanation: least, slate and stale share the letters a, e, l, s, t. tea, eat and ate share a, e, t. bus matches nothing and gets a bin of its own. The bins come in the order of their first words: least, then tea, then bus.
onto uses the same three kinds of letter as ton, but it has two o's and four letters, so it is not a rearrangement. It goes in its own bin.

hints: Take slate and least. If you sort the letters of each word alphabetically, what do you get?
Every rearrangement of the same letters sorts to the same string, and words with different letters never do. So the sorted letters work as a label for the bin.
Now you need to go from a label to its bin in one step, while keeping bins in the order they were first created. Which structure maps a key to a list?

Walk the words once. For each word, build its label (sorted letters, or 26 letter counts joined into a string). Look the label up in a map of label → bin. If it is missing, create an empty bin, add it to the map and to your result list. Then append the word to its bin.
bruteForce: For each word, compare it with the first word of every bin so far, using a letter-count check like the one in Same Letter Tiles. Put it in the first bin that matches, or start a new bin.

If most words are different, each word is compared with almost every bin, so this costs about n² comparisons. With 10,000 words that is around 50 million word comparisons, each reading up to 20 letters.

js: * @return {string[][]} bins, in order of first appearance

tests.note: empty words are rearrangements of each other
empty word keeps its own bin
same set of letters, different counts: defeats a letter-set key
equal letter-code sums: defeats a sum-of-letters key
duplicate word stays in its bin twice
longest words, differ in one letter

js: const binOf = new Map(); // sorted letters -> that bin
bins.push(binOf.get(label)); // same list object, so order is kept
py: bins.append(bin_of[label])  # same list object, so order is kept
walkthrough: The brute force compares words with each other. Instead, give every word a label that is the same for all its rearrangements and different for everything else. Then grouping is just "put each word in the bin with its label", one map lookup per word.
Sorting the letters makes a good label. Trace [least, tea, slate, eat, bus, stale, ate]:
• stale → bin 1, ate → bin 2. Result: [[least, slate, stale], [tea, eat, ate], [bus]].

The label must capture how many of each letter, not just which letters. A set of letters puts aab with abb, and a sum of letter codes puts ad with bc. Sorted letters, or a string of 26 counts, get both right.
solution.timeWhy: Each of the n words is sorted once, where L is the longest word (at most 20). A 26-count label makes it O(n · L).
solution.spaceWhy: The map and the bins together hold every word and one label per bin.
solution.takeaway: To group items that are "the same up to some change", compute a canonical key that erases the change (here, sort the letters), then group with a hash map from key to list. It turns pairwise comparisons into one lookup per item.
